current_example.title: Example: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

q-49890.name: Question 1
q-49890.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/2817662752008c41b76d1beb9bec73907f55d836524fe48c583997670421f70b.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=2{x}^{2},$ for $x\in [-2,\frac{5}{2}],$ and the horizontal line $y=-1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-49890.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from $x=-2$ to $x=\frac{5}{2}$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/e1774466f020515d3296f2e48fda0a61154bddbfd2285a67c97bdc7e35b60da5.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2{x}^{2}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{5/2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{5/2}[\,(2{x}^{2})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{5/2}(2{x}^{2}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{5/2}(4{x}^{4}+4{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49890.html:
Question 1
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2, for x∈[−2,52], and the horizontal line y=−1 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=−1, as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−25/2(4x4+4x2+1)dx
b
π∫−21(4x4+4x+1)dx
c
π∫−25/24x4dx
d
π∫−125/2(4x4+4x2+1)dx
e
π∫−25/2(2x2+4x+1)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from x=−2 to x=52 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=−1, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=2x2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫−25/2[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫−25/2[(2x2)−(−1)]2dx=π∫−25/2(2x2+1)2dx=π∫−25/2(4x4+4x2+1)dx.
q-49890.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line

q-50020.name: Question 2
q-50020.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/d27538da9cf9ebb39324477a9c3e9eabd950b648507ebc616a11d5c8a6054a19.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ for $x\in [0,2],$ and the horizontal line $y=-1$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $y=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50020.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/94d3f7e76db23c387366024bdd5dbb25f8adddc25d78bb3fc81f5900b4128fcf.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y={x}^{3}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,({x}^{3})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{6}+2{x}^{3}+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

q-50020.html:
Question 2
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3, for x∈[0,2], and the horizontal line y=−1 is rotated 360∘ about the line y=−1, as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−20(2x3+1)dx
b
π∫02(x6+2x3)dx
c
π∫20(4x−x3)dx
d
π∫−20(x6+1)dx
e
π∫02(x6+2x3+1)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=2 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=−1, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=x3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫02[(x3)−(−1)]2dx=π∫02(x3+1)2dx=π∫02(x6+2x3+1)dx.
q-50020.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line

q-120535.name: Question 3
q-120535.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/8fa5e5b2300c3395d48f5355352cd6ece7477f3bae8e8c185f0f869fa197b0e9.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x$ and the horizontal line $y=2$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-120535.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x & =2 \\ {x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x-2 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}(x-2)+(x-2) & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+1)(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/5a1821ff500c901d9f072fe56101f17e579018d0710543c4a2e371214894725c.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(2)-({x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+x)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2-x+2{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120535.html:
Question 3
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3−2x2+x and the horizontal line y=2 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫03(x3−2x2+x)2dx
b
π∫02(2−x+2x2−x3)2dx
c
2π∫03(2−x+2x2−x3)2dx
d
π∫02(2−x+2x2−x3)dx
e
2π∫02(x2−2x+1)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

x3−2x2+x=2x3−2x2+x−2=0x2(x−2)+(x−2)=0(x2+1)(x−2)=0

So, the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=2 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=x3−2x2+x, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫02[(2)−(x3−2x2+x)]2dx=π∫02(2−x+2x2−x3)2dx.
q-120535.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line

q-50022.name: Question 4
q-50022.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/1066e10a5a9860e371ca2895ec39f7cdce4e000d5cca9f3b478f57cd890d647a.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{1}{x},$ for $x\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ and the horizontal line $y=\frac{1}{2}$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=\frac{1}{2},$ as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50022.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from $x=\frac{1}{2}$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/6d4c086c9a3a99609728bc7c53f5a28ac86431e5c37e2b87bcfd3031a32aa470.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=\frac{1}{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=\frac{1}{x}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{[\,(\frac{1}{x})-(\frac{1}{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}{(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1/2}^{2}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-50022.html:
Question 4
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=1x, for x∈[12,2], and the horizontal line y=12 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=12, as shown above. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫1/22(1x2−1x+14)dx
b
π∫12(1x2−14)dx
c
π∫12(−1x+14)dx
d
π∫1/22(1x2+14)dx
e
π∫1/22(1x2+1x−14)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from x=12 to x=2 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=12, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=1x.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫1/22[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫1/22[(1x)−(12)]2dx=π∫1/22(1x−12)2dx=π∫1/22(1x2−1x+14)dx.

q-50007.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/848b73762d79b0b7b898f3c011e4118256b5fca37fa9d702313bc16da04b4c3d.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=2{x}^{2},$ for $x\in [0,1],$ and the horizontal line $y=2$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=2.$ Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50007.worked_solution:
First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/3b634be23e06f6038e00b91f27eadacd1d1bcc51516d741786cc433a1ce731ce.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=2{x}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(2)-(2{x}^{2})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(4{x}^{4}-8{x}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-2{x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-50007.html:
Question 5
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2, for x∈[0,1], and the horizontal line y=2 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=2. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
4π∫01(2x4−x2+1)dx
b
4π∫01(x4+2x2+1)dx
c
2π∫01(4x2+2)dx
d
2π∫01(2x4+2x2+2)dx
e
4π∫01(x4−2x2+1)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we are given that the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=1 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=2x2, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫01[(2)−(2x2)]2dx=π∫01(4x4−8x2+4)dx=4π∫01(x4−2x2+1)dx.
q-50007.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Horizontal Line

q-81681.name: Question 6
q-81681.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/c21d4794aeedcc70fe037a936724d2708a484d43c457b2d120927f86f1fa6ffc.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x-2$ and the horizontal line $y=-2$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=-2.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-81681.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x-2 & =-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/e785138362c91f9034d90ee9d923fc818cd299b3ee5d6d25eb1bf40cabc2f2b0.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={x}^{2}-2x-2,$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=-2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-2)-({x}^{2}-2x-2)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2x)^{2}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{4}-4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}-{x}^{4}+\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}\text{ })|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi ([\frac{1}{5}(2)^{5}-(2)^{4}+\frac{4}{3}(2)^{3}\text{ }]-[0]) \\  & =\pi (\frac{32}{5}-16+\frac{32}{3}) \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81681.html:
Question 6
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x2−2x−2 and the horizontal line y=−2 is rotated 2π radians about the line y=−2. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
8π3
b
16π15
c
14π15
d
6π5
e
4π5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

x2−2x−2=−2x2−2x=0x(x−2)=0

So, the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=2 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=x2−2x−2, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=−2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫02[(−2)−(x2−2x−2)]2dx=π∫02(−x2+2x)2dx=π∫02(x4−4x3+4x2)dx=π(15x5−x4+43x3 )|02=π([15(2)5−(2)4+43(2)3 ]−[0])=π(325−16+323)=16π15.

q-353047.name: Question 7
q-353047.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/ad089d39428498123469a2ac7895f7d04b8b3ff9dac18a1698462bfc7fabae99.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/975f68d06bb52e162ad792987899509f4090c03ec1b55af6335982a2951f6bbf.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=4-(x-1)^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=5.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,5-(4-(x-1)^{2})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(1+(x-1)^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(1+2(x-1)^{2}+(x-1)^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}((x-1)^{4}+2(x-1)^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi (\frac{1}{5}(x-1)^{5}+\frac{2}{3}(x-1)^{3}+x)\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{3}+2-(-\frac{1}{5}-\frac{2}{3}+0)) \\  & =\pi (\frac{43}{15}+\frac{13}{15}) \\  & =\frac{56\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-85996.name: Question 8
q-85996.problem: The region enclosed by the curve $y={e}^{x},$ the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=1,$ and the horizontal line $y=3$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $y=3.$ Find the volume of the resulting solid.
q-85996.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/72b701d2404e1acdcfba6b1994588419afc8246de6df8bf50e93baca0051df6a.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1$ along the $x$-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/89d6b6d2d65f161353da5fea9175aaf780f0fdc38405b855fbbc033349a484db.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y={e}^{x},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=3.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\,(3)-({e}^{x})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{(3-{e}^{x})}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(9-6{e}^{x}+{e}^{2x})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(9x-6{e}^{x}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}\text{ })|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi ([9-6e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}\text{ }]-[-6+\frac{1}{2}]) \\  & =\pi (\frac{29}{2}-6e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(29-12e+{e}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/73fc1e2cad0969a629e2c2c4a55ce8ac66c16b67fe2984e8b75dc6aa3a5eeace.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=1,$ and

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{[\,(\sqrt{4-x})-(1)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}((4-x)-2\sqrt{4-x}+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(5-x-2\sqrt{4-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi (5{\int }_{0}^{3}\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x+2{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{4-x}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\pi (5x{|}_{0}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{3}+\frac{4}{3}(4-x)^{3/2}{|}_{0}^{3}) \\  & =\pi ((15-0)-(\frac{9}{2}-0)+\frac{4}{3}(1-8)) \\  & =\pi (15-\frac{9}{2}-\frac{28}{3}) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-81661.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the region bounded by the curve y=4−x and the horizontal line y=1 from x=0 to x=3, as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 360∘about the line y=1.

a
 9π
b
 92π
c
 3π
d
 76π
e
 73π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, note that the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=3 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=1, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=4−x.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫03[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫03[(4−x)−(1)]2dx=π∫03((4−x)−24−x+1)dx=π∫03(5−x−24−x)dx=π(5∫03dx−∫03xdx+2∫034−xdx)=π(5x|03−x22|03+43(4−x)3/2|03)=π((15−0)−(92−0)+43(1−8))=π(15−92−283)=7π6.

q-352955.name: Question 10
q-352955.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/0e402d36061211a9e51df852f7fa595eb212e5c6ce9b3d43a2d53f9bea1fedd3.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=(x-1)^{4}$ and the horizontal line $y=1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $y=1.$ Find the volume $V$ of the resulting solid. Do not round the answer.

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-352955.worked_solution:
First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{4} & =1 \\ x-1 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=2$ along the $x$-axis. 

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/2a2e4be26d18e408bf6e4580c72ec2f3c08eed1750d38e0716f06a32d3c03e7c.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the lower function $y=(x-1)^{4},$ and

- *leaves* through the upper function $y=1.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{upper function})-(\text{lower function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,1-(x-1)^{4}\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(1-2(x-1)^{4}+(x-1)^{8})\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(x-\frac{2}{5}(x-1)^{5}+\frac{1}{9}(x-1)^{9}\text{ })|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi ([2-\frac{2}{5}(1)^{5}+\frac{1}{9}(1)^{9}\text{ }]-[0-\frac{2}{5}(-1)^{5}+\frac{1}{9}(-1)^{9}\text{ }]) \\  & =\frac{64\pi }{45}.\end{aligned}
$$

V=
64π45​

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line by solving the following equation: (x−1)4=1x−1=±1x=0,2

So, the limits of integration are from x=0 to x=2 along the x-axis.

To determine which is the lower function and which is the upper, let's draw our vertical arrow.

The vertical arrow

  • enters the region through the lower function y=(x−1)4, and

  • leaves through the upper function y=1.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(upper function)−(lower function)]2dx=π∫02[1−(x−1)4]2dx=π∫02(1−2(x−1)4+(x−1)8)dx=π(x−25(x−1)5+19(x−1)9 )|02=π([2−25(1)5+19(1)9 ]−[0−25(−1)5+19(−1)9 ])=64π45.

q-120810.name: Question 11
q-120810.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/7eb8812e90e4862a3658773186fe3809b212d58d5d22613fac6d9067ae4ccbc9.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ the vertical line $x=e,$ and the horizontal line $y=0$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=e,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-120810.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,⟹\,x={e}^{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/f0ddb5b21bdff9cbed426abed5bf9b94c4c4c4d742e2eb90dcdb92895c2adf3a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={e}^{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=e.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[\,(e)-({e}^{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(e-{e}^{y})^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2y}-2{e}^{y+1}+{e}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120810.html:
Question 11
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=ln⁡x, the vertical line x=e, and the horizontal line y=0 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=e, as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01(e2y+2ey+e2)dy
b
π∫01(e2y−2ey+e2)dy
c
π∫01(ey−e)dy
d
π∫01(e2y+2ey+1+e2)dy
e
π∫01(e2y−2ey+1+e2)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=ln⁡x⟹x=ey

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=ey, and

  • leaves through the right function x=e.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(e)−(ey)]2dy=π∫01(e−ey)2dy=π∫01(e2y−2ey+1+e2)dy.
q-120810.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

q-120816.name: Question 12
q-120816.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/5d154a914d58f5b695adec9dd873ac067ba8280a4fefffd4f2f5559ff5ee04da.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{1}{1-x},$ the vertical line $x=2,$ and the horizontal line $y=-2$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=2,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-120816.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=\frac{1}{1-x}\,⟹\,x=1-\frac{1}{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=-2$ to $y=-1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/239113c4d2bbca26c694796f6f17bd26bebf47697dad53f7af832088213fd4c9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=1-\frac{1}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}{[\,(2)-(1-\frac{1}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}{(1+\frac{1}{y})}^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}(1+\frac{2}{y}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120816.html:
Question 12
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=11−x, the vertical line x=2, and the horizontal line y=−2 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−2−1(1−1y)dy
b
π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy
c
π∫−2−1(1+4y+4y2)dy
d
π∫−2−1(1−2y+1y2)dy
e
π∫−2−1(1+1y)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=11−x⟹x=1−1y

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=−2 to y=−1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=1−1y, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫−2−1[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫−2−1[(2)−(1−1y)]2dy=π∫−2−1(1+1y)2dy=π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy.
q-120816.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

q-50017.name: Question 13
q-50017.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/293593a043a7713d87a2f8ad8a2eaecee26b34288e4662bb4b2fce834e703e56.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ the vertical line $x=-1$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50017.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/600ef6d7265add5c669a29394e45facae040292ce19caad9dcae390979b604b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=\sqrt[3]{y}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt[3]{y})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}+2{y}^{1/3}+1)\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-50017.html:
Question 13
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3, the vertical line x=−1 and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−10(2y1/3+1)dy
b
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy
c
π∫−11(−y2/3+2y1/3)dy
d
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3)dy
e
π∫−10(y2/3+1)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=x3⟹x=y3

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=y3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(y3)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(y3+1)2dy=π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy.
q-50017.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

q-120837.name: Question 14
q-120837.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/68359143b50b4d6187f2d50793b1d3cb4b48656f1996cd222cb5d07f666b535e.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=-1-x,$ the vertical line $x=-3,$ and the horizontal line $y=0$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-3,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-120837.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=-1-x\,⟹\,x=-1-y
$$

 

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=-3$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1-y & =-3 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/73d5da7e1bd4b409574f6e9ab034dde51012eb956b3ea72a3529f7d432fe781d.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-3,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=-1-y.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-1-y)-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2-y)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4y+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120837.html:
Question 14
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=−1−x, the vertical line x=−3, and the horizontal line y=0 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−3, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
∫02(y2+2y+2)dy
b
π∫01(2−y)dy
c
∫03(y2−y+2)dy
d
π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy
e
π∫03/2(y2+4y+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=−1−x⟹x=−1−y

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=−3 by solving the following equation:

−1−y=−3y=2

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=2 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=−1−y.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫02[(−1−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫02(2−y)2dy=π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy.

q-50081.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/421d588cd290294cf6471704f2459c22b00c8b47756b808e9da267a8007792b2.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ and the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=2,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
q-50081.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

 

We take the positive sign since $x\ge 0.$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=2$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}} & =2 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=8$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/c762c0e41cf8862535e5241a00149fdc6e409c3f79630a411cff73fcd11759b0.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{[\,(2)-(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}-2)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}(\frac{y}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

q-50081.html:
Question 15
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2 and the vertical lines x=0 and x=2 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01(y4−2y2+4)dy
b
π∫02(y2−2)dy
c
π∫08(y2+2)dy
d
π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy
e
π∫08(4y2+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=2x2⟹x=y2

We take the positive sign since x≥0.

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=2 by solving the following equation:

y2=2y=8

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=8 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y2, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫08[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫08[(2)−(y2)]2dy=π∫08(y2−2)2dy=π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy.

q-86058.name: Question 16
q-86058.problem: Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=\sqrt[3]{y},$ the vertical line $x=3,$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=3.$
q-86058.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/47b612a3e08ff24055cbffa7d53fb337f1905ec861abd3a8e535088d383162cb.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/1927874f5eca0c18b7b61b37d0e6fac5198ec9dcf89205763e88570287330292.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt[3]{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=3.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(3)-(\sqrt[3]{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[3-\sqrt[3]{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}-6{y}^{1/3}+9)\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2/3}\,\text{d}y-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{1/3}\,\text{d}y+9{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi (\frac{3{y}^{5/3}}{5}{|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{9{y}^{4/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}+9y{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi [(\frac{3}{5}-0)-(\frac{9}{2}-0)+(9-0)] \\  & =\frac{51\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={y}^{2}+1,$ the vertical line $x=5,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=5.$

$V=$
{{field-1}}
q-353068.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersection of the curve and the line $x=5$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+1 & =5 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/e83c5729ef5db920a0b451a8571ad84f45d2b4e950ab831ced0da2c0a12cea50.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={y}^{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=5.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,5-({y}^{2}+1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(16-8{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(16y-\frac{8}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (32-\frac{64}{3}+\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =\frac{256\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-120906.worked_solution:
Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left function and which is the right, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/8a17502c300fae56e9f2e1706d23a3e5a7d3233eebff9a77958d117a0135adb0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=6\sqrt{y}+1.$

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(6\sqrt{y}+1)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{y}+2)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24\sqrt{y}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24{y}^{1/2}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(36\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+24\cdot \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}+4y)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(18(1)^{2}+16(1)^{3/2}+4(1))-0] \\  & =38\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

q-81786.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/4643824b623d5325f53407147f086a95073db91be0148381780668c420ec7c45.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={e}^{y},$ the vertical line $x=e,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=e.$
q-81786.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=e$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y} & =e \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/93fd0875ea2ba1d1d92bb781a61cfb114ac88b7d240cd825b4842f686f7c760f.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={e}^{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=e.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(e)-({e}^{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[e-{e}^{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2}-2{e}^{y+1}+{e}^{2y})\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y+1}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}y\,{|}_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{y+1}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{{e}^{2y}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi (({e}^{2}-0)-2({e}^{2}-e)+(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\pi (-{e}^{2}+2e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{(4e-{e}^{2}-1)\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(-1+4e-{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
